As some general guides for gaming on linux were requested lately I though I try myself on one. Please excuse if this doesn't fit here or I unknowingly break some rules of conduct on voat...pretty new. So be kind.... ;)

Choosing a distribution

While this seems to be one of the most asked questions it's also one of the lesser important ones. Don't think too much about it. Afraid the truth is that choosing the correct distro for yourself is nothing you can do right at the start and also nothing others can help you with. It depends far too much on your personal preferences and you need a bit of experience with linux first to understand the differences of distros. So as first distro just pick one you seem to like..but be aware that you might want to switch after a year or so. Also don't give too much on the opinion of other people on what is the best distro..what might be a good distro for one person is a terrible choice for another.

Also I would recommend to not start with the more "difficult" distros right away. Linux is a new operating system for you and there will be enough things to learn. No need to make it even more complicated right at the start. Of course I don't want to say any of the "advanced" distros are bad...it's just easier to use them if you already know how filesystem permission work, how to easily edit files, know some basic commands of the shell...

One thing that needs to be mentioned here is that there are a lot of specialized distros out there made for exactly one purpose. Stay away fro those at the start. You will not be able to get gaming to work on Kali linux..that distro is not meant for gaming at all. Nor will you get it to work on Alpine linux..again that distro has a very different purpose. Stick to the major and general purpose distros at the start.

Not sure how to explain this now...at a first glimpse the differences between distros are not really very huge. And with first glimpse I mean what new users probably expect. All major distros come with a large repository of programs to install that contains the most used ones. Hardware support is about the same in all distros. You can install (almost) every desktop environment on every distribution. Games will work in every "major" distribution the same. The problem I have here is that in fact there are huge differences between the distros..each is a own Operating system. Just those difference lie much deeper than you usually care about at the start. It won't matter for you that the executable of VLC distributed by fedora doesn't work on debian...you just use VLC of debian. The available programs are (almost) the same..they are just not exchangeable between distros.

But lets talk about the differences a bit.

While hardware support is the same in all distros hardware detection is not! On some distros you might have to tell the distro yourself what driver modules you want to load while other distros have a extensive hardware detection that hardly needs you to do anything. The documentation of the distro usually helps you out there.

Graphics hardware support: All major distros allow installing the proprietary graphics drivers. But it differs how involved this is. On ubuntu it's usually only clicking "install addition drivers" in a pop-up at system start while on debian it involves adding some non-free repositories, installing the drivers from there and then making some minor edits to text files. Also the driver versions available differ between distros. One thing is common for all though...you install the drivers through their package manager. As far as I am aware only openSuse tumbleweed suggest using the drivers directly from the nvidia page...though with altered install instructions but I count tumbleweed to the moe advanced distros already. All other distros recommend to use the preconfigured drivers of their repositories. Check the documentation for your distro to install them.

Most distros have a default desktop environment. While they usually all allow installing and using other environments as well the default one will be usually the best supported one with disto specific setup tools integrated in the desktop and such.

Steam support: While officially ubuntu is the supported platform for steam it practically works on every major distro. The difference is that in case something breaks on ubuntu Valve feels bound to fix it with a patch while on other distros the distros itself fix it. What is faster is not that easy to say...steam broke on ubuntu several times as well and some distros are actually faster in fixing such issues than even valve. No matter what distro you pick, check the websit and documentation of your distro what is the preferred way of installing steam on it. A lot distros have steam in their package manager in a way that includes all fixes needed to get it to run. This should be generally preferred over installing directly from the steam website. Also it should be mentioned that SteamOS is based off debian, not ubuntu. So even valve doesn't follow it's own "supported" platform suggestion. ;)

32/64 bit: This question is easy to answer...the only reason you might want a 32 bit version of a distro is becasue your processor doesn't support 64 bit. In every other case you really want the 64 bit version...that means on almost all processors that aren't older than a decade. And no, it's not only about RAM. The 64 bit version also makes use of advanced processor instruction and extended processor registers...so even with less than 4GB RAM you want the 64 bit version. As a rule o thumb...if you ask this question you want 64 bit.

Finally a short list of distros with a slight focus on gaming. Of course this lit contains my views a bit so take it with a grain of salt. Many people will disagree with some points probably.

  • CentOS : Community version of Red hat (Sorry, no experience with it)

  • Debian : stable, huge repository, good documentation. Free software policy so installing non-free software like the proprietary nvidia drivers requires adding additional repositories.

  • Fedora : Red hat derivative (Sorry, no experience)

  • Kubuntu : Ubuntu flavour with KDE/Plasma as default desktop

  • Linux Mint : Derivative of ubuntu with additions for more pleasent user experience. Documentation a bit lacking but the ubuntu documentation works in most places

  • LMDE : Linux mint debian edition, derivative of debian with mint additions for better user experience. Documentation a bit lacking but debian docs work usually.

  • Lubuntu : Ubuntu flavour with lxde/lxqt as default desktop

  • OpenSuSE : Community version of SuSE, stable, all-in-one configuration tools, good documentation (and in addition good german documentation in case that's you native language)

  • Ubuntu : Large community to help out, easy setup of hardware, official steam platform, lots of documentation (And most good but have to be careful with things like ask ubuntu, not all answers there are...of adequate quality). Hard to make any future predictions due to ubuntu's practise of going their own ways but a solid choice for gaming at the moment.

  • UbuntuGNOME : Ubuntu flavour with gnome as default desktop

  • Xubuntu : Ubuntu flavour with Xfce as default desktop

One additon that really has to be mentioned as most people probably will have heard about it: SteamOS

I didn't include steamOS in the list above as it is not a distro meant for a desktop PC. It starts in steam's full picture mode. In case you want to setup a box for playing in the living room without the usual desktop needs steamOS might be a good choice for you. And steamOS allows dropping back to a gnome desktop but to really make it a usable desktop system a lot of tinkering and installing would be needed.

The Voat Goat is actually an :after selector, so changing the background image of the image element won't do anything, as that is "visibility: hidden". Instead, try targeting "#header-banner > a:after". The code should be:

#header-banner > a:after {
 background-image: url( %Link to the image% );
}

I would recommend putting this inside the "@media (min-width: 871px)" declaration, so it only affects tablets and desktops. I'd be more than happy to help, if you'd like. A great way to check out the CSS rules is to right click the element you want to change, and select "Inspect Element." This works really well in Chrome and Firefox, less so in Safari and Internet Explorer.

Now, knowing that, you have to do a special trick in order to target the element's "hover" state. I greatly prefer Chrome for this task, so that's what I'll be most able to provide a tutorial for, as follows. If you find the line of code that represents the item you're targeting, right click on that, and select "Force element state", then select ":hover". In the right column, you should now see something that has ":hover" at the end of the highlighted selector. For example, in the case of the "Top" sorting button, you should see the following:

.tabmenu li.disabled a.contribute:hover, .tabmenu li.disabled a:hover, .tabmenu li.selected a.contribute, .tabmenu li.selected a.contribute:hover, .tabmenu li.selected a:hover {
 background: rgba(246,246,246,1);
 color: #444;
 border-width: 0 1px;
 border-radius: 3px;
 border-color: transparent;
}

Changing the background of the "rgba" value should be what you want, here. Right now, it's set to 246,246,246, which is a light gray color. If you want (and again, this is easiest in Chrome, I find), you can change that by clicking on the color box right next to the text "rgba" and select a new color and transparency value. Once you have that, you'll need to copy that code along with the "@media (min-width: 871px)" and put that in your CSS. You can remove any rules that are already existing, because it would just overwrite the old rules with the exact same rules. Don't forget to add curly brackets for the "@media (min-width: 871px)" bit, or else it won't work correctly. It should read something like:

@[]media (min-width: 871px) {
 .tabmenu li.disabled a.contribute:hover, .tabmenu li.disabled a:hover, .tabmenu li.selected a.contribute, .tabmenu li.selected a.contribute:hover, .tabmenu li.selected a:hover {
 background: rgba(30, 79, 207, 1);
 }
}

Important note: because of Voat's comment formatting, I have to enter two hard brackets "[]" after the @ symbol, otherwise it tries to make it a reference to a user named "media" like Twitter would ("@media"); remove the brackets and that code should work perfectly.
